va_siesta_boulder.blurb: Siesta Boulder is one lone block beside the Blue Ridge Parkway in the Charlottesville area, high in the hills at roughly 3,100 feet. A broad, steep roof is the feature that draws people, and the dozen problems here are all bouldering. The spread is wide for such a small spot: a couple of easy warm-ups, a handful in the V3 to V4 range, a cluster of problems between V6 and V8, and one very hard line at the top end. It is a short uphill hike into the woods from the road, so it suits a quick session or a stop on a day spent bouldering along the parkway.

va_teahupo_o_boulder.blurb: Teahupo'o Boulder sits in Mill Creek Nature Park near Blacksburg, in the Beach section, and is the first block you meet when following the path up the east side of the creek toward the waterfalls. It is a big overhanging boulder with plenty of variety, holding twelve problems that are all bouldering. Grades run from easy ones around V1 and V2 through a middle band of V4 to V8, and the top end reaches into double digits. That range makes it worth a visit for both a moderate session and for people chasing hard, steep lines.

va_tilt_boulder.blurb: Tilt Boulder is one of the first blocks you reach in the Middle Boneyard at Grayson Highlands in southwest Virginia, a little higher up the hill from several better-known boulders. Its name comes from the long slanted stripes running across the rock. This is a friendly boulder for newer climbers, with a dozen bouldering problems that are mostly easy to moderate, a few around V4 to V5, and one harder line near V6. The best lines tend to be on the left-hand overhang. The Middle Boneyard has a reputation for being one of the warmer corners of the park when the weather turns cold.

va_title_fight_boulder.blurb: Title Fight Boulder is a large, slightly overhanging block in the Cascades bouldering zone near Blacksburg, in southwest Virginia. The route in is a walk up the creek trail and then a short climb up a hillside through a gap in the rhododendron. It is regarded as one of the best boulders around, and enough problems are packed onto it to fill a day by itself: twelve in all, from an easy V1 through a solid group in the V3 range to several V6 and V7 lines. Bring pads, since the standout problems are tall and committing.

wa_alien_wall.blurb: Alien Wall is a south-facing wall at Osborn Bay, just south of Electric City by Banks Lake in central Washington, with views over the water. It is the first wall you meet as you head up the trail, and it offers sport climbing on a mix of face climbing and a gently overhanging section that leads to a roof. Of the twelve routes, most fall in the 5.9 to 5.11 range: a lone 5.8, a couple at 5.9, five at 5.10 and three at 5.11, plus one 5.12 project-level line. The south-facing exposure means it catches plenty of sun.

wa_deadhead_wall.blurb: Deadhead Wall is the biggest cliff in the small hanging valley of Burge Hollow, on the east side of Burge Mountain near Tonasket in Okanogan County. It faces southwest, stands roughly 40 to 70 feet tall and stretches about 300 feet, with rock that climbers rate highly. All twelve routes are sport climbs, with a sizable group around 5.10, a few 5.9s, a couple of easier 5.7s and two 5.11s at the top end. The setting is forested, with a couple of seasonal ponds on the canyon floor.
wa_deadhead_wall.approach: A short walk of under five minutes from the trailhead: follow the cattle trail beside the fence line south, drop into the canyon, and pass the ponds. The wall is on your left beyond the second pond.
